semin-durr:1-1.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: {المص}: The discussion of the disjointed letters (al-aḥruf al-muqaṭṭaʿa) has been given at the beginning of this work.
[Translator's note: The source has «الموضوع» ("subject/topic"); "work" renders the evident sense.]

semin-durr:2-2.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: {كتابٌ}: It may be a khabar (predicate) of the letters before it, or the khabar of an implied mubtadaʾ (subject), i.e.: "it is a Book"; this is how al-Zamakhsharī construed it. It is also possible that «كتاب» is a mubtadaʾ, «أُنْزِل» its naʿt (adjective), and «فلا تكن» its khabar, with the fāʾ redundant (zāʾida) according to the view of al-Akhfash, i.e.: a Book described as sent down to you — let there be no constraint in your breast from it. This is very far-fetched. What stands in place of the agent (nāʾib fāʿil) in «أُنْزِل» is a pronoun referring to the Book. The preposition-phrase may not be it, lest the adjective clause be left without a referring pronoun.
His saying: «منه» is attached (mutaʿalliq) to «حَرَجٌ». «مِنْ» is causal, i.e.: constraint because of it; you say: حَرِجْتُ منه, i.e. I was straitened because of it. It may also be attached to something omitted, as an adjective of it, i.e.: constraint existing and issuing from it. The pronoun in «منه» may refer to the Book, which is the apparent sense; it may refer to the sending-down indicated by «أُنْزِل», or to the warning or the conveying, both indicated by the context of the speech, or to the denial implied by the meaning. The prohibition is in form directed at the constraint, but what is meant is the one from whom it issues, for emphasis in forbidding that, as though it were said: do not engage in causes from which constraint arises. It is of the type «لا أُرَيَنَّك ههنا» ("let me not see you here"): the prohibition is directed at the speaker while what is meant is the one addressed, as though he said: do not be in my presence, so that I see you. Similar is: {فَلاَ يَصُدَّنَّكَ عَنْهَا مَن لاَّ يُؤْمِنُ} [Ṭā Hā: 16].
His saying: «لتنذرَ به»: concerning what this lām is attached to there are three views. The first: that it is attached to «أُنْزِل», i.e. it was sent down to you for warning. This is the view of al-Farrāʾ, who said: "The lām in «لتنذرَ» is joined to his saying «أُنْزِل» by way of advancing and postponing, the implied order being: a Book sent down to you that you may warn by it — so let there be no…" Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Ḥūfī and Abū al-Baqāʾ followed him. On this view the prohibitive clause is parenthetical between the cause and what it causes; that is what al-Farrāʾ meant by his saying "by way of advancing and postponing". The second: that the lām is attached to what the khabar of the being (kawn) is attached to, since the implied form is: let no constraint be settled in your breast for the sake of warning. Thus the Shaykh [Abū Ḥayyān] said, from Ibn al-Anbārī, for he said: "Ibn al-Anbārī said: the implied form is 'let there be no constraint in your breast from it so that you may warn by it'; so he made it attached to what «في صدرك» is attached to; and the author of «al-Naẓm» likewise attached it to that; on this view the clause is not parenthetical." I say: what al-Wāḥidī reported from Ibn al-Anbārī's own text on this is that the lām is attached to the being (kawn), and from the author of «al-Naẓm» that the lām has the meaning of «أن»; their texts will come, if Allah wills. So it may be that each of them had two statements.
The third: that it is attached to the being (kawn) itself, which is the position of Ibn al-Anbārī, al-Zamakhsharī and the author of «al-Naẓm», according to what the Shaykh reported.
Abū Bakr ibn al-Anbārī said: "The lām may be connected to the being, in the sense: let there be nothing in your breast, so that you may warn — as one man says to another: 'Do not be unjust, so that your companion may pay his debt'; so you make the lām of kay depend on the being." Al-Zamakhsharī said: "If you ask: to what is «لتنذر» attached? I say: to «أُنْزِل», i.e. it was sent down for your warning by it; or to the prohibition, because if they did not frighten him he would warn them; likewise, if he knew that it is from Allah, certainty would embolden him to warn." The Shaykh said: "His saying 'to the prohibition' apparently means that it is attached to the prohibitive verb, so that it is attached to his saying «فلا يكن»; and there is a disagreement [among them] about attaching a genitive phrase to it and its governing an adverb, which rests on whether the defective (nāqiṣa) «كان» indicates an event (ḥadath) or not: whoever says it indicates an event allows that, and whoever says it does not indicate one forbids it." I say: al-Zamakhsharī was preceded to this view; indeed, there is nothing in his wording indicating that it is attached to «يكون»; rather he said "to the prohibition", and he may mean the sense it contains. And granting that, the correct view is that all the defective verbs indicate an event except «ليس»; I have set out proofs for that and established statements of scholars that bear witness to its correctness, such as the statement of Sībawayh and his peers, elsewhere than this place.
The author of «al-Naẓm» said: "There is another view in it, namely that the lām has the meaning of أَنْ, the sense being: let your breast not be straitened nor weak from warning by it. The Arabs put this lām in the place of «أَنْ», as in His saying, Exalted is He: {يُرِيدُونَ أَن يُطْفِئُواْ نُورَ الله} [al-Tawba: 32] and in another place: {لِيُطْفِئُواْ} [al-Ṣaff: 8], and the two have one meaning." I say: this is an utterly worthless view: how can a particle specific to verbs occur in the place of another specific to nouns?
[Translator's note: The author's objection presumably treats this lām as the preposition (which governs nouns), even though it is followed by a verb in the subjunctive through an implied أَنْ.]
His saying: {وذكرى} may be in the position of a nominative, an accusative or a genitive. The nominative has two explanations. The first: that it is conjoined (maʿṭūf) to «كتابٌ», i.e. a Book and a reminder, i.e. a reminding; so it is a noun of maṣdar (ism maṣdar). This is the view of al-Farrāʾ. The second of the two nominative explanations: that it is the khabar of an implied mubtadaʾ, i.e.: it is a reminder. This is the view of Abū Isḥāq al-Zajjāj. The accusative has three explanations. The first: that it is accusative as a maṣdar by a verb from its own root, the implied form being: وتَذَكَّرْ ذكرى, i.e. a reminding. The second: that it is in the position of an accusative, conjoined to the position of «لتنذرَ», whose position is accusative; it is then conjoined according to the sense, just as an explicit ḥāl is conjoined to an interpreted ḥāl, as in His saying, Exalted is He: {دَعَانَا لِجَنبِهِ أَوْ قَاعِداً أَوْ قَآئِماً} [Yūnus: 12]; it is then a mafʿūl li-ajlihi (object of purpose), as you say: «جئتك لتكرمَني وإحساناً إليّ» ("I came to you that you might honour me, and as a kindness to me").
The third: Abū al-Baqāʾ said, and he began with it: "It is a ḥāl from the pronoun in «أُنْزِل», and what is between them is parenthetical." This is an oversight, for the wāw prevents that: how can the wāw come before an explicit ḥāl?
The genitive also has two explanations. The first: conjunction with the maṣdar formed from the implied «أَنْ» after the lām of kay together with the verb, the implied form being: for warning and reminding. The second: conjunction with the pronoun in «به»; this is the view of the Kufans. What makes it acceptable is that «ذكرى» stands for a maṣdar particle, namely «أَنْ», and a verb; had «أَنْ» been stated explicitly, omitting the preposition with it would have been acceptable; so it is better than «مررت بك وزيدٍ» ("I passed by you and Zayd"), since the implied form is: that you may warn by it and by your reminding.
As for «للمؤمنين», the lām may be added to the object to strengthen it, because the governing word is secondary (farʿ), the implied form being: and that you may remind the believers. The second: that it is attached to something omitted, because it is an adjective of ذكرى.

semin-durr:3-3.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: {مِّن رَّبِّكُمْ}: Two views are possible in it. The first: that it is attached (mutaʿalliq) to أُنْزِل, with «مِنْ» marking the beginning of a figurative extent. The second: that it is attached to something omitted, as a ḥāl (circumstantial), either from the relative noun or from its referring pronoun which stands in place of the agent (nāʾib fāʿil).
His saying: {مِن دُونِهِ أَوْلِيَآءَ}: «من دونه» may be attached to the verb before it, the meaning being: do not turn from Him to others, such as devils and soothsayers. The second: that it is attached to something omitted, because it was originally an adjective of أولياء; when it was placed first it was made accusative as a ḥāl. Al-Zamakhsharī's interpretation inclines to this, for he said: "i.e. do not take as allies, besides Him, devils of mankind and jinn, so that they carry you off to whims and innovations." The pronoun in «دونِه» may — and this is the apparent sense — refer to «ربكم»; that is why al-Zamakhsharī said: "besides Allah"; it may refer to the relative «ما», and it may refer to the sent-down Book, the meaning being: do not turn from it to the abrogated books. Al-Jaḥdarī read: «ابتَغُوا» with the dotted ghayn, from ibtighāʾ (seeking). Mālik ibn Dīnār and Mujāhid read: «ولا تبتغوا», also from ibtighāʾ.
[Translator's note: The source has «الاتغاء», evidently a slip for «الابتغاء».]
His saying: {قَلِيلاً مَّا تَذَكَّرُونَ}: The counterpart of this has been given in His saying, Exalted is He: {فَقَلِيلاً مَّا يُؤْمِنُونَ} [al-Baqara: 88], namely that «قليلاً» is the adjective of an omitted maṣdar (verbal noun), i.e.: a little reflecting do you reflect; or the adjective of an omitted adverb of time as well, i.e.: for a little time do you reflect. The maṣdar or the adverb is then accusative by the verb after it, and «ما» is redundant (zāʾida) for emphasis. This is a plain, clear i'rab. Al-Ḥūfī allowed it to be the adjective of an omitted maṣdar of his saying «ولا تَتَّبعوا», i.e.: do not follow, besides Him, allies with a little following. This is weak, because its implication (mafhūm) would be that they are not forbidden from following much; but that is known from the side of meaning, so it has no implication.
Ibn ʿAṭiyya reported from Abū ʿAlī that «ما» is a maṣdar particle connected to the verb after it, and confined himself to that much; but it needs completing. So someone said: "«قليلاً» is then the adjective of an omitted time, and that omitted time is in the position of a nominative as a fronted khabar, while the maṣdar «ما» with what follows, interpreted as a maṣdar, is a postponed mubtadaʾ; the implied form is: for a little time is your reflecting, i.e. their reflecting occurs only at some times. Its parallel is: زمناً قليلاً قيامُك ('for a little time is your standing')." It has been said that this «ما» is negative; this is far-fetched, because, according to the Basrans, what follows «ما» does not govern what precedes it; and even granting that, the meaning would become: you do not reflect a little, which is of no use. This is as will come in His saying, Exalted is He: {كَانُواْ قَلِيلاً مِّن الليل مَا يَهْجَعُونَ} [al-Dhāriyāt: 17] according to those who make it negative.
There is a view there that cannot apply here, namely that «ما» is a maṣdar particle, and it with what follows is in the position of a nominative as the agent of «قليلاً», which is the khabar of «كان», the implied form being: they were [such that] little was their sleeping. Here, however, that is not possible, because «قليلاً» cannot validly be made accusative by his saying «ولا تتَّبعوا» so that «ما تذكَّرون» could be made nominative by it.
Nor may «قليلاً» be a ḥāl from the agent of «تَتَّبعوا» with «ما تذكَّرون» nominative by it, since the meaning would become: they were forbidden from following while their reflecting was little, and that is not what is meant.
The two brothers [Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī] and Ḥafṣ read: «تَذَكَّرون» with one tāʾ and the dhāl undoubled; Ibn ʿĀmir with two tāʾs and the dhāl undoubled; and the rest with one tāʾ and the dhāl doubled. These are clear; their meaning has been given in al-Anʿām.

semin-durr:4-4.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: {وَكَم مِّن قَرْيَةٍ أَهْلَكْنَاهَا}: Concerning «كم» there are two views. The first: that it is in the position of a nominative (marfūʿ) as a mubtadaʾ (subject), its khabar (predicate) being the clause after it; «من قرية» is a tamyīz (specification), and the pronoun in «أهلكناها» refers to the meaning of كم. Here it is the declarative كم (khabariyya), expressing multitude, the implied form being: and many of the towns We destroyed. Abū al-Baqāʾ reported from someone that he made «أهلكناها» an adjective of قرية, with the khabar being His saying «فجاءها بأسنا»; he said: "This is an oversight, because the fāʾ prevents that." I say: even if someone claimed it was redundant (zāʾida) according to the view of al-Akhfash, his claim would not be accepted, because al-Akhfash makes it redundant only when there is a need for its redundancy.
The second: that it is in the position of an accusative (manṣūb) by ishtighāl (preoccupation of the verb), through an implied verb explained by what follows; the verb is construed as coming after «كم», because كم has the front of the sentence (ṣadr al-kalām); the implied form is: "how many a town We destroyed — We destroyed it". It has the front of the sentence for two reasons. The first: its resemblance to the interrogative «كم». The second: that it is the opposite of «رُبَّ», because it expresses multitude and «رُبَّ» expresses paucity; so the opposite was treated like its opposite, just as they treat a counterpart like its counterpart.
A muḍāf must be omitted in the speech because of His saying, Exalted is He: «أو هم قائلون»; so we are compelled to construe something omitted. Then some construed it before «قرية», i.e.: how many of the people of a town; and some construed it before «ها» in «أهلكناها», i.e.: We destroyed its people. This is nothing, because constructions are supplied only for need, and need does not call for construing this muḍāf in these two places mentioned, since the destruction of a town can fall upon the town itself: towns are destroyed by sinking into the earth, demolition, burning, drowning and the like. It is needed only at His saying «فجاءها», so that the pronoun in His saying «هم قائلون» can refer to it; so it is construed: and how many a town We destroyed, and Our might came upon its people. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "If you ask: do you construe the muḍāf, namely 'people', before «قرية» or before the pronoun in «أهلكناها»? I say: the muḍāf is construed only for need, and there is no need, for a town is destroyed just as its people are destroyed. We construed it only before the pronoun in «فجاءها» because of His saying «أو هم قائلون»."
The apparent sense of the verse is that the coming of the might was after the destruction and immediately following it, because the fāʾ gives that; but what actually happens is the coming of the might, and after it the destruction occurs. Some grammarians said: the fāʾ comes with the meaning of the wāw, so it does not express sequence, and they counted this verse among such cases; this is weak. The majority answered this in two ways. The first: that it is on the omission of "willing", i.e.: We willed to destroy it, as in His saying: {إِذَا قُمْتُمْ إِلَى الصلاة} [al-Māʾida: 6], {فَإِذَا قَرَأْتَ القرآن} [al-Naḥl: 98], and "When one of you enters the privy, let him name Allah."
The second: that the meaning of "We destroyed it" is: We forsook them and did not grant them success, and their destruction arose from that; so the effect was expressed in place of its cause, and that is a wide field. There are weak answers, among them: that the fāʾ here is explicative, as in: "He performed ablution, so he washed his face, then his hands," so it is not for immediate sequence. Among them: that it is for sequence in the speech only, as though He informed about many towns that He destroyed them, and then said: and of their affair was the coming of the might. And among them is what al-Farrāʾ said, namely that the destruction is the coming of the might and the coming of the might is the destruction; since they are inseparable, it does not matter which you put first in order, as in your saying: "He insulted me and so did me wrong" and "He did me wrong and so insulted me": the wrong and the insult are one thing. So these are six views.
Know that when a muḍāf is omitted and the muḍāf ilayhi put in its place, two considerations are open to you. The first: to take account of the omitted word; the second — and it is the more common — not to take account of it. Both have been combined here: He did not take account of the omitted word in His saying «أهلكناها فجاءها» and took account of it in His saying «أو هم قائلون». That is if we construe the omission before «قرية»; but if we construe the omission before the pronoun of «فجاءها», then He took account only of the omitted word, which is not the more common.
His saying: «بَيَاتاً» has three views. The first: that it is accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial), and it is originally a maṣdar (verbal noun): بات يبيتُ بَيْتاً وبَيْتَةً وبَيَاتاً وبَيْتُوتة. Al-Layth said: "al-baytūta is your entering into the night." So His saying «بياتاً» means: spending the night. They also allowed it to be a mafʿūl lahu (object of purpose), and to be in the ruling of an adverb. Al-Wāḥidī said: "His saying بياتاً: i.e. by night." The apparent sense of this wording is that it is an adverb, unless it is said that he meant to explain the meaning.
His saying: {أَوْ هُمْ قَآئِلُونَ}: this clause is in the position of an accusative, conjoined to the ḥāl. «أو» here is for variety (tanwīʿ) and nothing else, as though it were said: Our might came to them sometimes by night, like the people of Lūṭ, and sometimes at the time of the midday rest, like the people of Shuʿayb. Is a ḥāl-wāw to be construed before this clause or not? There is a disagreement among the grammarians. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "If you say: one does not say «جاء زيد هو فارس» without a wāw, so what about His saying, Exalted is He, «أو هم قائلون»? I say: some grammarians construed the wāw as omitted, and al-Zajjāj rejected that and said: 'If you said: «جاءني زيد راجلاً أو هو فارس» ("Zayd came to me on foot or riding") or «جاءني زيد هو فارس», you would not need a wāw, because the mention [i.e. the pronoun] has referred back to the first.' The correct view is that when it is conjoined to a ḥāl before it, the wāw is dropped as being heavy, because of two conjunctions coming together, since the ḥāl-wāw is the conjunctive wāw borrowed for connection. So your saying «جاء زيد راجلاً أو هو فارس» is eloquent speech occurring according to its rule, whereas «جاءني زيد هو فارس» is vile." The Shaykh said: "As for the 'some grammarians' whom al-Zamakhsharī left unnamed, it is al-Farrāʾ.
As for al-Zajjāj's statement [regarding] the two examples, 'you would not need the wāw in it because the mention has referred back to the first', there is vagueness in it. Making it precise: its entry is forbidden in the first example and allowed in the second; so the absence of need is not equal in both, because in the first it is due to the prohibition of entry, and in the second due to its frequency [of omission], not its prohibition." I say: as for its prohibition in the first example, it is because the grammarians stated explicitly that when a conjunction enters a circumstantial clause, the ḥāl-wāw is forbidden from entering it; the reason for that is verbal resemblance, and because the ḥāl-wāw is originally conjunctive.
Then the Shaykh said: "As for al-Zamakhsharī's saying 'the correct view is…' to the end, his reasoning is not correct, because the ḥāl-wāw is not a conjunction such that mentioning it would entail two conjunctions coming together. For were it a conjunction, what precedes it would have to be a ḥāl so that it conjoins a ḥāl to a ḥāl; its occurring where there cannot be a ḥāl proves that it is not a conjunctive wāw, nor is the meaning of a conjunctive wāw noted in it. You say: «جاء زيد والشمسُ طالعةٌ» ('Zayd came while the sun was rising'), and 'Zayd came' is not a ḥāl so that a circumstantial clause could be conjoined to it. Rather this wāw differs from the conjunctive wāw in every respect; it is one of the kinds of wāw, just as it comes for the oath, where it is not conjunctive, as when you say: «والله ليخرجَنَّ» ('By Allah, he will surely go out')." I say: Abū al-Qāsim [al-Zamakhsharī] did not claim that the ḥāl-wāw is conjunctive; rather he claims that its origin is conjunction. His saying "borrowed for connection" indicates that: had it remained conjunctive, he would not have said "borrowed". So his saying indicates that it left conjunction and was used for another meaning, but was given the ruling of its origin in its being prevented from accompanying another conjunction. As for calling it a conjunction, that is in consideration of its origin. A parallel is the wāw of "with" (maʿiyya): they stated explicitly that its origin is the conjunctive wāw, then it was used for accompaniment. So likewise the ḥāl-wāw: there is nothing to prevent its origin being the conjunctive wāw.
Then the Shaykh said: "As for his saying 'vile', it is not vile. He based it on [the view] that when the circumstantial clause is nominal and contains a pronoun of the one it describes, dropping the wāw from it is anomalous (shādhdh); in that he followed al-Farrāʾ. But it is not anomalous; rather it is frequent in verse and prose." I say: al-Farrāʾ and Abū Bakr ibn al-Anbārī preceded Abū al-Qāsim in calling this wāw a conjunction. Al-Farrāʾ said: "«أو هم قائلون» has an implied wāw in it; the meaning is: We destroyed it, and Our might came to it by night or while they were taking their midday rest; they found one conjunction right after another heavy; had it been said, it would have been correct." I say: it has been stated above that the Shaykh reported that the wāw is forbidden in this example and did not relate any disagreement; yet this statement of al-Farrāʾ, "had it been said, it would have been correct", explicitly disagrees with him. Abū Bakr said: "The ḥāl-wāw was left implied because its meaning is clear, as the Arabs say: «لقيت عبد الله مسرعاً أو هو يركض» ('I met ʿAbd Allāh hurrying, or he was running'), dropping the wāw because they are safe from ambiguity, since the mention has referred back to the one described by the ḥāl; and because «أو» is a conjunction and the wāw is likewise, they found it heavy to combine two conjunctions, so they dropped the second."
I say: this is an explicit statement from these two imams of what Abū al-Qāsim mentioned. I cited the text of these two imams only to make known his acquaintance with people's statements, and that he does not bring anything outside the terminology of the people of knowledge, as he [the Shaykh] accuses him of more than once.
«قائلون» is from al-qaylūla (the midday rest). One says: قال يَقيل قَيْلولة, so he is قائل, like بائع. Al-qaylūla is rest and ease in the heat of the middle of the day, even if there is no sleep with it. Al-Layth said: it is the sleep of midday. Al-Azharī said: "al-Qaylūla is rest even if there is no sleep in it, as proven by His saying, Exalted is He: {أَصْحَابُ الجنة يَوْمَئِذٍ خَيْرٌ مُّسْتَقَرّاً وَأَحْسَنُ مَقِيلاً} [al-Furqān: 24], and in Paradise there is no sleep." I say: there is no proof in what he mentioned, because المقيل here has left its original meaning for mere residing, as proven by the fact that resting at midday in the heat is not meant either; so it has left its original meaning, by our view and yours, for what I have told you. al-Qaylūla is a maṣdar, and similar to it are: al-thāʾila, al-qayl and al-maqīl.
[Translator's note: «الثائلة» is as written in the source; the usual form listed among these maṣdars is «القائلة».]

semin-durr:5-5.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: {فَمَا كَانَ دَعْوَاهُمْ}: They allowed two views for «دعواهم». The first: that it is the noun (ism) of «كان» and «إلا أَنْ قالوا» its khabar (predicate). There is a flaw in this, in that the less definite was made the ism and the more definite was made the khabar; you have understood that at the beginning of al-Anʿām, at {لَمْ تَكُنْ فِتْنَتُهُمْ} [verse 23]. The second: that «دعواهم» is a fronted khabar and «إلا أن قالوا» a postponed ism. Al-Zamakhsharī and Makkī ibn Abī Ṭālib mentioned that, and al-Farrāʾ and al-Zajjāj preceded them to it, al-Zajjāj preferring it. But that is problematic in view of another rule the grammarians mention, namely that in this chapter, whenever the case-marking of the ism and the khabar is not visible, the ism must come first and the khabar after, as in: كان موسى صاحبي ("Mūsā was my companion") and ما كان دعائي إلا أن استغفرتُ ("my supplication was nothing but that I sought forgiveness"). They said: because they are like the object and the agent; whenever the case-marking is hidden, each keeps to its rank. This verse is of the kind we are discussing, so how can that be claimed for it — indeed, how can al-Zajjāj prefer it? I have seen al-Zajjāj's words here, and an answer for this place can be taken from them. He said: "Except that the preferred form, if «الدعوى» were in the position of a nominative, would be to say: فما كانت دعواهم; since He said «كان دعواهم», it indicated that الدعوى is in the position of an accusative; yet it is permissible to make الدعوى masculine even if it is nominative." I say: from here it is said: the masculine form of the verb is a contextual indicator (qarīna) favouring attribution of the verb to «أن قالوا»; had it been attributed to الدعوى, «كانت» would have been preferable, as he said. It is close to your saying «ضربت موسى سلمى» ("Salmā struck Mūsā"), where you put the object first on the indication of the verb's feminine form. Moreover, there is another indicator, namely that the more definite has more right to be the ism than the less definite.
الدَّعْوى may mean supplication (duʿāʾ) and may mean claim (iddiʿāʾ); what is meant by it here may be both together, and it may also mean confession. Of its use meaning supplication is what al-Khalīl related: «اللهم أشركنا في صالح دعوى المسلمين» ("O Allah, give us a share in the righteous supplication of the Muslims"), meaning in their righteous supplication; and they recited:
2139 - وإنْ مَذِلَتْ رِجْلي دعوتُك أشتفي ... بدَعْواكَ مِنْ مَذْلٍ بها فتهونُ
(And if my foot goes numb, I call upon you, seeking cure by calling you from the numbness in it, and it eases.)
And of it is His saying, Exalted is He: {فَمَا زَالَت تِلْكَ دَعْوَاهُمْ} [al-Anbiyāʾ: 15]. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "It may also be: their crying for help was nothing but this saying of theirs, because one does not seek help against Allah the Exalted from other than Him — from their saying: 'Their cry was: O Kaʿb!'" Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "The verse may mean: their claims that were in the state of their unbelief came to nothing but confession, as in the poet's saying:
2140 - وقد شهدَتْ قيسٌ فما كان نصرُها ... قتيبةَ إلا عضَّها بالأباهم
(Qays was present, and its help to Qutayba was nothing but biting its thumbs.)"
«إذ» is accusative by «دعواهم».
His saying: {إِنَّا كُنَّا}: «كنَّا» with its khabar is in the position of a nominative as the khabar of «إنَّا»; إنَّ with what falls in its scope is in the position of an accusative, being quoted by «قالوا»; «قالوا» with what falls in its scope has no grammatical position, since it occurs as the ṣila (relative clause) of أَنْ; and أَنْ with what falls in its scope is in the position of a nominative or an accusative, according to what was said above about its being the ism or the khabar.

semin-durr:6-6.t: His saying, Exalted is He: {الذين أُرْسِلَ إِلَيْهِمْ}: What stands in place of the agent (nāʾib fāʿil) is the preposition and its genitive noun.

semin-durr:7-7.t: And His saying, Exalted is He: {بِعِلْمٍ}: is in the position of a ḥāl (circumstantial) from the agent, and the bāʾ is for accompaniment, i.e.: We will surely relate to the messengers and those to whom they were sent, while We are invested with knowledge. Then He emphasised this meaning with His saying {وَمَا كُنَّا غَآئِبِينَ}.

semin-durr:8-8.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: {والوزن يَوْمَئِذٍ الحق}: «الوزنُ» is a mubtadaʾ (subject), and concerning the khabar (predicate) there are two views. The first: it is the adverb, i.e.: the weighing is existing or settled on that day, i.e. the day when We question the messengers and those to whom they were sent. The clause to which «إذ» is annexed was omitted and the tanwīn substituted for it. This is the position of the majority, contrary to al-Akhfash. On this view there are three views concerning «الحق». The first: that it is a naʿt (adjective) of الوزن, i.e. the true weighing on that day. The second: that it is the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, as though it were the answer to an implied question from someone saying: what is that weighing? So it was said: it is the truth, not falsehood. The third: that it is a badal (substitute) from the pronoun latent in the adverb. This is strange; Makkī mentioned it.
The second of the two views on the khabar: that the khabar is «الحق». On this view «يومئذ» has two views. The first: that it is accusative as an adverb governed by «الوزن», i.e.: the weighing takes place on that day. The second: that it is a direct object by extension (ʿalā al-saʿa). This second is very weak and unnecessary. When Abū al-Baqāʾ mentioned that «الحق» is the khabar and made «يومئذ» an adverb of الوزن, he said: "On this view it may not be an adjective, lest it entail separating the relative [i.e. the maṣdar] from its ṣila." I say: and where is the separation? For in the Quranic construction «الحق» comes only after the relative is complete with its ṣila, and when the relative is complete with its ṣila it may be qualified. You say: «ضَرْبُك زيداً يوم الجمعة الشديدُ حسنٌ» ("Your hard beating of Zayd on Friday is good"), and الشديد is an adjective of ضربك. If he imagined that the adjective's place is to come right after the described noun and adjoin it, so that it is as if placed first in construction and the separation occurs in construction, this is not to be heeded, because those governed words are part of the completion of the relative, so there is nothing but the relative. And granting that he believed this, what also prevents it is that the mubtadaʾ would be left without a khabar: if you make «يومئذ» an adverb of الوزن and «الحق» its adjective, where is its khabar? So even if it were safe from the impediment he mentioned, it would have this other impediment.
[Translator's note: "relative" (mawṣūl) here refers to the maṣdar «الوزن», which grammarians treat like a relative noun with its complements as its ṣila.]
Makkī went on at length mentioning the construing of «الحق» before «يومئذ» and after it according to the preceding analyses; this is unnecessary, because in the Quran we are bound to its arrangement as it comes. He also mentioned that it could be accusative, meaning that had it been read so it would have been permissible; this too is unnecessary.
As for موازين, there are two views on it. The first: that it is the plural of ميزان, the instrument by which things are weighed; it was put in the plural because each person has a balance specific to him, as has come in exegesis, or it was put in the plural with regard to the many deeds, expressing what occupies a place by the place. The second: that it is the plural of موزون (what is weighed), namely the deeds; the plural is then evident.

semin-durr:9-9.t: His saying, Exalted is He: {بِمَا كَانُواْ}: is attached (mutaʿalliq) to «خسروا»; «ما» is a maṣdar particle, and «بآياتنا» is attached to «يظلمون», placed before it for the sake of the verse-ending (fāṣila). «يظلمون» is made transitive with the bāʾ either because it implies the meaning of denial (takdhīb), as in {كَذَّبُواْ بِآيَاتِنَا} [Āl ʿImrān: 11], or because it implies the meaning of rejection (jaḥd), as in {وَجَحَدُواْ بِهَا} [al-Naml: 14].

semin-durr:10-10.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: {وجَعَلْنا لكم}: It may have the meaning of «خلق» ("created"), and so take one object; the two prepositional phrases are then attached (mutaʿalliq) to the making, or to something omitted as two ḥāls (circumstantials) from «معايش», because had they come after it they could have been two adjectives. It may also be the jaʿala of transformation (taṣyīr), taking two objects: the first is «معايش» and the second one of the two prepositional phrases, while the other is either a ḥāl, and so attached to something omitted, or attached to the making itself — and this is the apparent view.
معايش is the plural of معيشة, about which there are three positions. The position of Sībawayh and al-Khalīl: that its pattern is mafʿula with ḍamma on the ʿayn, or mafʿila with kasra on it. On the first, the ḍamma was turned into a kasra and moved to the fāʾ [i.e. first radical] of the word. The analogy of al-Akhfash's view in this kind of word is that the letter is changed, not the vowel; so معيشة is anomalous for him, since it ought to have been said مَعُوشة. But on our saying that its origin is مَعْيِشة with kasra on the ʿayn, there is no anomaly in it. The position of al-Farrāʾ is that its pattern is mafʿala with fatḥa on the ʿayn; this is nothing. المعيشة is a noun for that by which one lives, i.e. is kept alive. It is originally a maṣdar (verbal noun) of عاش يعيش: عَيْشاً and عِيْشة — the Exalted said: {فِي عِيشَةٍ رَّاضِيَةٍ} [al-Ḥāqqa: 21] — and معاشاً — the Exalted said: {وَجَعَلْنَا النهار مَعَاشاً} — and مَعِيشاً; Ruʾba said:
2141 - إليك أشكو شِدَّةَ المعيشِ ... وجُهْدَ أعوامٍ نَتَفْنَ ريشي
(To you I complain of the hardship of living, and the strain of years that have plucked my feathers.)
The generality [of readers] read «معايش» with a plain yāʾ. Khārija broke away and transmitted from Nāfiʿ «معائش» with hamza. The grammarians said: this is a mistake, because for them only a word in which the long-vowel letter is additional is given hamza, as in صحائف and مدائن; but in «معايش» the yāʾ is radical, because it is from العَيْش. Al-Fārisī said, from Abū ʿUthmān [al-Māzinī]: "The origin of taking this reading is from Nāfiʿ," and he said: "He did not know what Arabic is." I say: the Arabs did the like of this; they put hamza in منائر and مصائب, plurals of منارة and مصيبة, whose origin is مناوِر and مصاوب. Sībawayh judged as mistaken whoever says مصائب, meaning by that that it is a mistake relative to departing from the beaten path, just as was quoted from him earlier, that he said: "Know that some of them err and say: «إنهم أجمعون ذاهبون»." He said: "And some of them bring it according to the origin and say: مصاوب and مناور, just as they said in the plural of مقال and مقام: مَقَاوِم and مَقاوِل, returning the ʿayn to its origin." He said: and the grammarians cited for that:
2142 - وإنِّي لَقَوَّامٌ مَقَاوِمَ لم يكن ... جريرٌ ولا مَوْلَى جريرٍ يقومُها
(I am one who stands much in places of standing in which neither Jarīr nor Jarīr's client would stand.)
The rationale of its hamza is that they likened the radical [to the additional] and imagined معيشة to be on the pattern of صحيفة, so they gave it hamza, as they put hamza in تِيْك. They said: a parallel to that in their likening the radical to the additional is their saying, in the plural of مَسِيل: مِسْلان, imagining it to be on the pattern of قضيب and قِضبان; and they said in its plural أَمْسِلة, as though they imagined it to be on the pattern of رغيف and أرغفة; yet the pattern of مسيل is mafʿil, because it is from the flowing (sayalān) of water. For مَسيل and أَمْسِلة they cited the saying of Abū Dhuʾayb al-Hudhalī:
2143 - بِوادٍ لا أنيسَ به يَبابٍ ... وأَمْسِلةٍ مَذانِبُها خَلِيفُ
(In a desolate valley with no companion in it, and watercourses whose channels are a path between hills.)
Al-Zajjāj said: "All the grammarians of Basra claim that its hamza is an error, and I know no rationale for it except the likening to صحيفة and صحائف; this reading should not be relied upon."
I say: Nāfiʿ was not alone in this reading; rather a group of eminent readers read it with him. It is transmitted from Ibn ʿĀmir, who read before a group of the Companions such as ʿUthmān, Abū al-Dardāʾ and Muʿāwiya — this has been mentioned before in al-Anʿām — and he read it before the appearance of solecism (laḥn), being a pure Arab. Zayd ibn ʿAlī also read it, and he had a share of eloquence and knowledge that few approach. Al-Aʿmash and al-Aʿraj also read it, and they suffice in precision and exactness. Al-Farrāʾ reported that changing this yāʾ, likening it to the yāʾ of صحيفة, has occurred, even if rarely.
His saying: {قَلِيلاً مَّا تَشْكُرُونَ} is like His saying: {قَلِيلاً مَّا تَذَكَّرُونَ} [al-Aʿrāf: 3].

semin-durr:11-11.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: {وَلَقَدْ خَلَقْنَاكُمْ ثُمَّ صَوَّرْنَاكُمْ ثُمَّ قُلْنَا}: People have differed about «ثم» in these two places. Some did not hold that it entails any sequence and treated it like the wāw, for our creation and our fashioning came after His saying, Exalted is He, to the angels «اسجدوا». Some said: it is for sequence, not in time but in the order of narration; there is no benefit in this. Some said: it is for temporal sequence, and this is its original meaning. And some said: the first is for temporal sequence and the second for sequence in narration. Those who say it is for [temporal] sequence in both places differed in their wording. Some of them said: that is on the omission of two muḍāfs, the implied form being: We created your father, then fashioned your father, then said — meaning by our father Ādam, peace be upon him. Temporal sequence here is evident with this construction. Some of them said: the address in «خلقناكم وصوَّرناكم» is to Ādam, peace be upon him; He addressed him in the plural form, though he is one, to honour him and because he is the origin of all; the sequence is also clear.
Some of them said: those addressed are the children of Ādam, but what is meant is their father. This is of the type of addressing one person while meaning another, as in His saying: {وَإِذْ نَجَّيْنَاكُم مِّنْ آلِ فِرْعَوْنَ} to its end, whereas those delivered and who were subjected to the evil punishment were their forebears. This is widespread in their language. They cited for that the poet's saying:
2144 - إذا افتخرَتْ يوماً تميمٌ بقوسها ... وزادَتْ على ما وطَّدَتْ مِنْ مناقب
فأنتم بذي قارٍ أمالَتْ سيوفُكمْ ... عروشَ الذين استرهنوا قوسَ حاجبِ
(If Tamīm one day boasts of its bow and adds to the glories it has established, then you — at Dhū Qār your swords toppled the thrones of those who took Ḥājib's bow in pledge.)
And this battle took place only among their forebears.
The sequence is also clear on this. Those who said that the first is for temporal sequence and the second for sequence in narration also differed in their wording. Some of them said: what is meant by the first address is Ādam and by the second his offspring; the temporal sequence is clear, and the second «ثم» is for sequence in narration. Some said: We created you in the loins of Ādam, then fashioned you in the wombs of your mothers. Some said: We created your spouses, then fashioned your bodies. This is strange; al-Qāḍī Abū Yaʿlā reported it in «al-Muʿtamad». Some said: We created you as drops of semen in the loins of men, then fashioned you in the wombs of women. And some said: We created you in the bellies of your mothers and fashioned you there after the creation by opening the hearing and sight; so the first «ثم» is for sequence in time and the second for sequence in narration.
His saying: {إِلاَّ إِبْلِيسَ}: its discussion has been given in al-Baqara. His saying «لم يكن»: this clause is resumptive (istiʾnāfiyya), because it is the answer to an implied question; this is as was said before about His saying «أبى» in al-Baqara. It was stated before that the pause is on إبليس. It was also said: the benefit of this clause is emphasis of what the exception brought out, namely the negation of Iblīs's prostration. Abū al-Baqāʾ said: "It is in the position of an accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial), i.e.: except Iblīs, while refusing to prostrate." This is like what he said before in al-Baqara, that «أبى» is in the position of an accusative as a ḥāl.

semin-durr:12-12.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: {أَلاَّ تَسْجُدَ}: Concerning this «لا» there are two views; the more apparent of them is that it is redundant (zāʾida) for emphasis. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "«لا» in «أن لا تسجد» is a connective (ṣila) [i.e. redundant], as shown by His saying, Exalted is He: {مَا مَنَعَكَ أَن تَسْجُدَ لِمَا خَلَقْتُ بِيَدَيَّ} [Ṣād: 75]; similar to it is {لِّئَلاَّ يَعْلَمَ أَهْلُ الكتاب} [al-Ḥadīd: 29], meaning ليعلم." Then he said: "If you ask: what is the benefit of its being added? I say: emphasising and affirming the meaning of the verb it enters upon, as though it were said: so that the knowledge of the People of the Book may be affirmed; and what prevented you from realising the prostration and binding yourself to it when I commanded you?" For the redundancy of «لا» they cited the poet's saying:
2145 - أبى جودُه لا البخلَِ واستعجلَتْ نَعَمْ ... به مِنْ فتى لا يمنع الجودَ نائلُه
(His generosity refused the "no" of stinginess, and "yes" hastened forth from a youth whose giving does not withhold generosity.)
«البخل» is transmitted in the accusative and the genitive. The accusative clearly indicates its redundancy, the implied form being: his generosity refused stinginess. In the genitive transmission, the apparent sense is that it does not indicate its redundancy. Yet there is no proof in this verse for the redundancy of «لا» even in the accusative transmission; it can be explained in two ways. The first: that «لا» is a direct object and «البخل» a badal (substitute) from it, because «لا» is said in refusing, so it conveys stinginess. The second: that it is also a direct object, and البخل a mafʿūl li-ajlihi (object of purpose), the meaning being: his generosity refused the word «لا» on account of stinginess, i.e. out of dislike of stinginess. The genitive transmission supports non-redundancy. Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ said: "The transmission in it is with «البخل» in the genitive, because «لا» is used in stinginess." They also cited for its redundancy another's saying:
2146 - أَفَعَنْكَ لا برقٌ كأنَّ وميضَه ... غابٌ تَسَنَّمَه ضِرامٌ مُثْقَبُ
(Is it from you — a lightning whose flash is like a thicket topped by a kindled blaze?)
He means: أفعنك برقٌ. The Shaykh explained it on the possibility that it is a conjunction with the conjoined omitted, the implied form being: is it from you, not from others? That «لا» in the verse is redundant is the position of al-Kisāʾī, al-Farrāʾ and Abū Isḥāq. What I mentioned, that «البخل» is a badal from «لا» and «لا» a direct object, is the position of al-Zajjāj. Someone related from Yūnus that he said: "Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ used to put «البخل» in the genitive and make «لا» annexed to it; he meant: his generosity refused the 'no' that belongs to stinginess, because «لا» may belong to stinginess and to generosity. The one belonging to stinginess is known; the one belonging to generosity is that if someone said to him 'withhold what is due' or 'do not give the poor' and he said 'no', it would be generosity." I say: he means that the iḍāfa is then for clarification, because «لا» had become shared, so he distinguished it by the iḍāfa and specified it thereby. A good portion on the redundancy of «لا» and people's statements about it has been given at the end of al-Fātiḥa.
A group claimed that «لا» in this noble verse is not redundant, but their wording differed in making its meaning sound. Some said: there is an omission in the speech by which the negation is sound, the implied form being: what prevented you, so that it compelled you not to prostrate? Some said: the meaning is: what drove you not to prostrate? Some: who commanded you not to prostrate? and: who told you not to prostrate? or: what called you not to prostrate? This is the strained effort of one who feels uneasy about attributing redundancy to the Quran. Its verification has been given before, and that redundancy is in a sense understood by the people of knowledge; otherwise, how could redundancy be claimed in the Quran in the general, everyday sense? No Muslim says that.
«ما» is interrogative, in the position of a nominative as a mubtadaʾ (subject), and the khabar (predicate) is after it, i.e.: what thing prevented you? «أَنْ» is in the position of an accusative or a genitive, because it is on the omission of the preposition, since the implied form is: what prevented you from prostrating? «إذ» is accusative by تسجد, i.e.: what prevented you from prostrating at the time of My commanding you to do it? His saying: {خَلَقْتَنِي مِن نَّارٍ}: this clause has no grammatical position, because it is like an explanation and clarification of the declarative [clause].

semin-durr:13-13.t:
And His saying, Exalted is He: {مِنْهَا}: and «فيها»: the pronoun refers to the Garden, because he was among its inhabitants. From Ibn ʿAbbās: they were in ʿAdn, not in the Garden of Eternity. It was said: it refers to the heaven, because it is narrated in exegesis that he whispered to the two of them while he was in the heaven. It was said: to the earth — he was commanded to leave it for the islands of the seas, and to enter the earth only like a thief. It was said: to the lofty rank and high station. And it was said: to the form and appearance he had, because he had a radiant face and it became dark. His saying «فاخرجْ» is an emphasis (tawkīd) of «اهبط», since it has its meaning.
His saying «فيها» has no implication (mafhūm), meaning that one should not imagine that it is permissible for him to be arrogant elsewhere. When someone took this implication into account, he needed to construe an omitted conjoined phrase, as in His saying: {تَقِيكُمُ الحر} [al-Naḥl: 81]; he said: "The implied form is: it is not for you to be arrogant in it nor elsewhere."

semin-durr:14-14.t: The pronoun in {يُبْعَثُونَ} refers to the children of Ādam, because the context indicates them, just as it indicated what the two pronouns in منها and فيها refer to, as stated before.

semin-durr:16-16.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: {فَبِمَآ أَغْوَيْتَنِي}: Concerning this bāʾ there are two views. The first: that it is the bāʾ of the oath; this is the apparent view. The second: that it is causal; al-Zamakhsharī began with it, saying: "«فبما أغويتني»: because of Your leading me astray, I will surely sit in wait for them." Then he said: "The meaning is: because of my falling into error, I will surely strive to lead them astray so that they become corrupt because of me, as I became corrupt because of them. If you ask: to what is the bāʾ attached, since its attachment to «لأقعدن» is barred by the lām of the oath — you do not say: «واللهِ بزيدٍ لأمرَّنَّ» ('By Allah, by Zayd I will surely pass')? I say: it is attached to the omitted verb of swearing, the implied form being: because You have led me astray, I swear by Allah I will surely sit, i.e.: because of Your leading me astray, I swear. The bāʾ may also be for the oath, i.e.: I swear by Your leading me astray that I will surely sit." I say: Abū Bakr ibn al-Anbārī preceded him to these two views and gave wording close to this wording.
The Shaykh said: "What he mentioned, that the lām prevents the attachment of the bāʾ to «لأقعدَنَّ», is not an agreed-upon ruling; rather there is a disagreement about it." I say: as for the disagreement, yes; but it is a weak disagreement by which Abū al-Qāsim [al-Zamakhsharī] is not bound. And the Shaykh himself said, at His saying, Exalted is He, {لَّمَن تَبِعَكَ مِنْهُمْ لأَمْلأَنَّ} [al-Aʿrāf: 18], in the reading of those who give kasra to the lām in «لمن», that the majority do not allow that; it will come to you explained, if Allah wills.
«ما» admits three views; the most apparent is that it is a maṣdar particle, i.e.: by Your leading me astray. The second: that it is interrogative, meaning that he asked about the cause by which He led him astray, saying: by what thing among things did You lead me astray? Then he began afresh a clause in which he swore, with his saying «لأقعدنَّ». This is weak according to some, or a poetic licence according to others, in that when the interrogative «ما» is in the genitive its alif is dropped, and it is retained only anomalously, as in their saying: عمَّا تسأل؟, or by poetic licence, as in the poet's saying:
2147 - على ما قام يَشْتِمني لئيمٌ ... كخنزيرٍ تمرَّغَ في رمادِ
(For what reason did a base man stand up to revile me, like a pig rolling in ashes?)
The third: that it is conditional; this is the view of Ibn al-Anbārī, and his text must be quoted. He said, may Allah have mercy on him: "«ما» may be construed as a conditional, the bāʾ being connected to the leading astray, and the implied fāʾ being the apodosis of the condition; the implied form is: by whatever thing You have led me astray, then I will surely sit in wait for them on Your path. So the fāʾ is left implied [in] the apodosis of the condition, as you leave it implied in your saying: «إلى ما أومأتَ إني قابلُه، وبما أمرت إني سامعٌ مطيع» ('to whatever you indicate, I accept it; and in whatever you command, I hear and obey')." What he said is very weak, for, granting that its meaning is sound, it is impossible from the standpoint of grammatical craft, because the fāʾ of the apodosis is dropped only by poetic licence, as in the poet's saying:
2148 - مَنْ يفعلِ الحسناتِ اللهُ يشكرُها ... والشرُّ بالشر عند الله مِثْلان
(Whoever does good deeds, Allah will thank them; and evil for evil is, with Allah, alike.)
i.e.: فالله. Al-Mubarrad did not allow that even as poetic licence, and he recited the mentioned verse as:
مَنْ يفعل الخير فالرحمن يشكره ... . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
(Whoever does good, the Most Merciful will thank him…)
So on Abū Bakr's view, his saying «لأقعدنَّ» is the answer of an omitted oath, and that implied oath with its answer is the apodosis of the condition; he construes the fāʾ as entering on the oath clause itself together with its answer, the implied form being: by whatever You have led me astray, then by Allah I will surely sit.
This completes his position.
His saying: «صراطَك»: concerning its accusative there are three views. The first: that it is accusative by removal of the preposition (bi-nazʿ al-khāfiḍ). Al-Zajjāj said: "There is no disagreement among the grammarians that «على» is omitted, as in your saying «ضُرِب زيدٌ الظهرَ والبطنَ» ('Zayd was struck on the back and the belly'), i.e. on the back and the belly." However, what al-Zajjāj said, although it appears to claim consensus, is weak, in that the omission of the preposition is not regular; rather it is restricted to poetic licence or anomaly, as in the poet's saying:
2149 - تمُرُّون الديارَ فلم تعوجوا ... . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
(You pass the dwellings and do not turn aside…)
[and his saying]:
2150 -. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... . . . . . . . . . . . . لولا الأسى لقضاني
(…were it not for grief, it would have finished me.)
[and his saying]:
2151 - فَبِتُّ كأنَّ العائداتِ فَرَشْنني ... . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
(So I spent the night as though the visiting women had spread me [on thorns]…)
The second: that it is accusative as an adverb (ẓarf), the implied form being: I will surely sit in wait for them on Your path. This too is weak, because «صراطك» is a specific (mukhtaṣṣ) adverb of place, and the verb does not reach a specific adverb of place by itself but only through «في». You say: صليت في المسجد ("I prayed in the mosque") and نمت في السوق ("I slept in the market"); you do not say صَلَّيْتَ المسجد, except in what is excepted in the books of grammar; and if anything else occurs, it is anomalous, as in their saying «رَجَع أدراجَه» ("he went back the way he came") and «ذهبت» with «الشام» specifically, or by poetic licence, as in the poet's saying:
2152 - جزى الله بالخيراتِ ما فعلا بكم ... رفيقَيْنِ قالا خَيْمَتَيْ أمِّ معبدِ
(May Allah reward with good things, for what they did for you, two companions who rested at midday in the two tents of Umm Maʿbad.)
i.e.: they rested at midday in the two tents. As a parallel to the verse in making a specific place accusative they cited another's saying:
2153 - لَدْنٌ بهزِّ الكفِّ يَعْسِل مَتْنَه ... كما عَسَل الطريقَ الثعلبُ
(Supple, quivering along its shaft at the shake of the hand, as the fox trots along the road.)
The grammarians cited this verse as a poetic licence. Ibn al-Ṭarāwa departed from the position of the grammarians and made «الصراط» and «الطريق» in these two places vague (mubham) places. This is a rejected view, because the specific among places is that which has bounds enclosing it and limits confining it, and الصراط and الطريق are of this kind. The third: that it is accusative as a direct object, because the verb before it, although intransitive, has been made to imply the meaning of a transitive verb; the implied form is: I will surely occupy Your straight path by sitting on it.

semin-durr:17-17.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: {ثُمَّ لآتِيَنَّهُمْ}: is a clause also conjoined to the answer of the oath. He stated that after sitting on the path he will come from these four directions. He varied the preposition, putting the first two in the genitive with «مِنْ» and the second two with «عن», for a subtle point that al-Zamakhsharī mentioned. He said, may Allah have mercy on him: "If you ask: how was it said 'from before them and from behind them' with the particle of beginning, and 'from their right and from their left' with the particle of passing beyond (mujāwaza)? I say: the verb is made to reach the mafʿūl fīhi (adverbial) in the same way as it is made to reach the direct object; so just as the particles of transitivity differ in that, they differ in this; it is usage that is taken [as heard] and not made a basis of analogy; one only examines the soundness of where it occurs. When we heard them say: 'he sat عن his right' and 'على his right', and 'عن his left' and 'على his left', we said: the meaning of 'على his right' is that he was established on the side of the right as something above is established on what it is above; and the meaning of 'عن his right' is that he sat keeping apart from the one on the right, not adjoining him, turned away from him. Then it became frequent until it was used for the one keeping apart and others, as we mentioned regarding تعالَ. Similar to it with the direct object is their saying: 'I shot على the bow, عن the bow and من the bow', because the arrow goes away from it and is above it when placed on its middle for shooting, and the shooting begins from it. That is why they said: 'he sat between his hands and behind him', with the meaning of في, because they are two adverbs for the verb; and 'from between his hands' and 'from behind him', because the action occurs in part of the two directions, as you say: 'I came from the night', meaning part of the night." I say: these are the words of one whose foot is firm in understanding the speech of the Arabs. The Shaykh said: "It is a statement with no harm in it," and so did not give it its due.
Then he [the Shaykh] said: "I say: He assigned 'before' and 'behind' the particle of beginning, which is more firmly established in coming, only because they are the directions from which the enemy most often comes and seizes his opportunity. He put 'before' ahead of 'behind' because it is the direction that indicates the enemy's boldness and valour in facing his opponent without fear of him, while 'behind' is the direction of treachery, deceit and the opponent's ignorance of who is assassinating him and seeking his heedlessness and inattention. He assigned the right and the left the particle indicating passing beyond, because they are not the directions from which the enemy most often comes; rather his coming passes beyond [them] to the direction that is more usual in that. The right was put before the left because it is the strong side in meeting the enemy, and with the right hand is striking and repelling; so the opponent who comes from its side is braver and more courageous, since he came from the side that is stronger in repelling, and the left is not like the right in strength and repelling.
الأيمان and الشمائل are the plurals of يمين and شمال, the two limbs [the right and the left hand]; in the plural of paucity they take the pattern afʿul; the poet said:
2154 - يأتي لها من أَيْمُنٍ وأَشْمُلِ ...
(He comes at her from right sides and left sides…)
الشمائل is used to express character and dispositions; you say: he has good شمائل (qualities). Good deeds are expressed by the right and bad deeds by the left, because they are the source of the two actions, good and bad.
They say: 'Put me in your right hand, not in your left'; the poet said:
2155 - أبُثْنى أفي يُمْنَى يديكِ جَعَلْتِني ... فَأَفْرحَ أم صَيَّرْتني في شِمالكِ
(O Buthayna, have you put me in your right hand, so that I rejoice, or placed me in your left?)
By that they allude to the greatness of one's standing with a person or its lowness. And he said:
2156 - رأيت بني العَلاَّتِ لمَّا تضافروا ... يَحُوزون سَهْمي بينهمْ في الشَّمائل
(I saw the half-brothers, when they banded together, gathering my share among them in the left hands.)
الشمائل is also the plural of شَمَال with fatḥa on the shīn, which is the [north] wind. Imruʾ al-Qays said:
2157 - وهَبَّتْ له ريحٌ بمختلف الصُّوى ... صَباً وشَمالٌ في منازِلِ قُفَّالِ
(And a wind blew upon it where the waymarks diverge — an east wind and a north wind — in the halting places of returning travellers.)
The alif in الشمال is additional; for this reason a hamza is also added to it after the mīm, so they say شَمْأَل, and before it, so they say شَأْمَل; what proves all this is its dropping in derivation: they say «شَمَلَت الريح» when it blows from the north."
[Translator's note: The source gives no closing quotation mark for the Shaykh's quotation; where it ends is not certain.]
His saying: {وَلاَ تَجِدُ أَكْثَرَهُمْ}: الوِجْدان here may have the meaning of meeting (encountering) or the meaning of knowing, i.e.: you will not find most of them grateful, or you will not know most of them to be grateful. So «شاكرين» is a ḥāl (circumstantial) on the first, and a second object on the second. This clause admits two views. The first: that it is resumptive (istiʾnāfiyya); the accursed one stated that because he supposed it, or because he knew it by some means. And it may fall within the scope of what precedes it in the answer to the oath, being conjoined to his saying «لأقعدَنَّ»: he swore to two affirmative clauses and one negative.

semin-durr:18-18.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: {مَذْءُوماً مَّدْحُوراً}: two ḥāls (circumstantials) from the agent of «اخرج», according to those who allow multiple ḥāls for a single owner of the ḥāl. For those who do not allow that, «مدحوراً» is an adjective of «مذؤوماً», or it is a ḥāl from the pronoun in the ḥāl before it, so that the two ḥāls are nested (mutadākhilān). مذؤوماً and مدحوراً are passive participles of ذَأَمه and دَحَره. As for ذَأَمه, one says with hamza: ذَأَمه يَذْأَمه, like رأَمه يَرْأَمُه; and ذامه يَذيمه, like باعه يبيعه, without hamza. On this is their saying: «لن يَعْدَمَ الحسناء ذاماً» ("A beautiful woman will not lack some fault"), transmitted with a quiescent hamza or with alif. On the second dialect is the poet's saying:
2158 - تَبِعْتُك إذْ عَيْني عليها غِشاوةٌ ... فلما انجلَتْ قَطَّعْتُ نفسي أَذِيْمُها
(I followed you while a veil was over my eye; when it cleared, I tore myself apart, reproaching it.)
The maṣdar (verbal noun) of the hamzated form is ذَأْم, like رَأْس. As for the maṣdar of the non-hamzated form, ذامٌ with alif has been heard in it, and Ibn al-Anbārī related ذَيْماً in it, like يَنْع. He said: "One says ذَأَمْتُ الرجل أَذْأَمُه, and ذِمْتُه أَذِيْمُه ذَيْماً, and ذَمَمْتُه أَذُمُّه ذَمَّاً, with one meaning." And he recited:
2159 - وأقاموا حتى انبرَوا جميعاً ... في مَقامٍ وكلُّهم مَذْؤُوْمُ
(They stayed until they all set forth in one standing-place, and every one of them was reproached.)
الذَّامُ is fault; from it is the proverb mentioned above: «لن يَعْدَمِ الحسناءُ ذاما», i.e. every beautiful woman must have some fault. They said: «أردتَ أن تَذيمه فمدحتَه» ("you wanted to fault him, and you praised him"), i.e. to find fault with him; [in the proverb] the ḥāʾ was changed to hāʾ. [Translator's note: The proverb is usually cited as «أردتَ أن تذيمه فمدهته», with hāʾ; the source cites it with ḥāʾ and then comments on the change.] It was said: الذام is contempt; ذَأَمْتُ الرجل, i.e. I held the man in contempt; al-Layth said so. It was said: الذام is blame; Ibn Qutayba and Ibn al-Anbārī said so.
The majority read «مَذْؤوماً» with hamza. Abū Jaʿfar, al-Aʿmash and al-Zuhrī read «مَذُوْمَاً» with one wāw and without hamza. It admits two views. The first — and one should not depart from it — is that it is the lightening of «مذؤوماً» in the well-known reading, by casting the hamza's vowel onto the quiescent dhāl and dropping the hamza, according to the established rule for lightening such words; so the pattern of the word became mafūl, because of the dropping of the ʿayn. The second: that this reading is taken from the dialect of those who say ذِمْتُه أَذيمه, like بِعْتُه أَبيعه; by right the passive participle in this dialect would be مَذيم, like مبيع. They said: but the wāw was substituted for the yāʾ, on the pattern of their saying «مكول» for «مكيل», although it is from الكيل. Like this reading in admitting both views is the saying of Umayya ibn Abī al-Ṣalt:
2160 - وقالَ لإِبليسَ ربُّ العبادِ ... [أن] اخرُجْ لعيناً دحيراً مَذُوْمَا
(The Lord of the servants said to Iblīs: Go out, accursed, banished, blamed.)
Al-Wāḥidī cited it for the dialect of ذامه with alif, يَذيمه with yāʾ; I wish he had made it admit the lightening from the hamzated dialect.
الدَّحْر is driving away and banishing. One says: دَحَره يَدْحَرُه دَحْراً ودُحوراً; from it is {وَيُقْذَفُونَ مِن كُلِّ جَانِبٍ دُحُوراً} [al-Ṣāffāt: 9], and Umayya's saying in the preceding verse «لَعيناً دحيراً», and also his saying:
2161 - وبإذنه سجدوا لآدمَ كلهمْ ... إلا لعيناً خاطِئاً مَدْحورا
(By His permission they all prostrated to Ādam, except an accursed, sinful, banished one.)
And another said:
2162 - دَحَرْتُ بني الحصيب إلى قَدِيدٍ ... وقد كانوا ذوي أَشَرٍ وفَخْرِ
(I drove the Banū al-Ḥaṣīb back to Qudayd, though they had been people of insolence and boasting.)
His saying: {لَّمَن تَبِعَكَ}: Concerning this lām and «مَنْ» there are two views. The more apparent: that the lām is the lām of preparation (tawṭiʾa) for an omitted oath, «مَنْ» is conditional, in the position of a nominative as a mubtadaʾ (subject), and «لأملأنَّ» is the answer to the oath indicated by the lām of preparation, while the apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ) is omitted because the answer of the oath takes its place.
The explanation of that has been given more than once. The second: that the lām is the lām of inception (lām al-ibtidāʾ), «مَنْ» a relative noun and «تبعك» its ṣila (relative clause), and it too is in the position of a nominative as a mubtadaʾ; «لأملأنَّ» is the answer to an omitted oath, and that omitted oath with its answer is in the position of a nominative as the khabar (predicate) of this mubtadaʾ; the implied form is: as for the one of them who follows you — by Allah, I will surely fill Hell with you. If you ask: where is the referring pronoun from the oath clause occurring as khabar of the mubtadaʾ? I say: it is included in His saying «منكم», because when a third-person and a second-person pronoun came together, the second person was made to prevail, as has been known more than once.
The fatḥa on the lām is the reading of the generality. ʿĀṣim, in the transmission of Abū Bakr [Shuʿba] through some of its chains, and al-Jaḥdarī read «لِمَنْ» with kasra, and it has been explained in three ways. The first — and Ibn ʿAṭiyya held it — that it is attached (mutaʿalliq) to His saying «لأَملأنَّ», for he said: "For the sake of those of them who follow you, I will surely fill"; the apparent sense of this is that it is attached to the verb after the lām of the oath. The Shaykh said: "That is impossible on the view of the majority that what comes after the lām of the oath does not govern what precedes it." The second: that the lām is attached to the blaming and the banishing, the meaning being: go out with these two attributes because of your followers. Abū al-Faḍl al-Rāzī mentioned it in the book «al-Lawāʾiḥ ʿalā Shādhdh al-Qirāʾa». I say: the question can come under the chapter of iʿmāl (competing governors), because each of مذؤوماً and مدحوراً, according to this speaker, requires this prepositional phrase in meaning, and the government would go to the second, as is the Basrans' preference, with omission from the first.
The third: that this prepositional phrase is a fronted khabar and the mubtadaʾ is omitted, its implied form being: for those of them who follow you is this threat; and «هذا الوعيد» ("this threat") is indicated by His saying «لأملأن جهنم», because this oath with its answer is a threat. This is what al-Zamakhsharī meant by his saying: "In the sense: for those of them who follow you is the threat, namely His saying «لأملأن جهنم», on the basis that «لأملأنَّ» is in the position of the mubtadaʾ and «لمن تبعك» its khabar." The Shaykh said: "If he meant the apparent sense of his words, it is an error according to the position of the Basrans, because His saying «لأملأنَّ» is a clause that is the answer to an omitted oath. Insofar as it is merely a clause, it may not be a mubtadaʾ; and insofar as it is the answer to the omitted oath, it is also impossible, because from that standpoint it has no grammatical position, whereas insofar as it is a mubtadaʾ it has a grammatical position; and a clause may not both have a grammatical position and have no grammatical position. That is absurd, because it would entail its being in the position of a nominative and not in the position of a nominative, with a governor entering upon it and no governor entering upon it, and that is inconceivable."
I say: after al-Zamakhsharī said "in the sense: for those who follow you is the threat, namely «لأملأنَّ»", how is it proper to hesitate after that and say "if he meant the apparent sense of his words"? How could he mean it when he himself explicitly stated his interpretation? As for his saying "on the basis that «لأملأنَّ» is in the position of the mubtadaʾ", he said that only because it indicates the threat that is in the position of the mubtadaʾ; so he attributed to what indicates what is attributed to what is indicated, from the side of meaning.
Also the Shaykh's saying "and insofar as it is the answer to the omitted oath…" to the end is a statement that burdens him unfairly, because he [al-Zamakhsharī] does not at all mean the answer clause alone; he means the oath clause in its entirety, and he made do with mentioning it [the answer] instead of mentioning its counterpart [the oath] because it is the one that is pronounced. Something resembling this last objection against him, and its answer, has been given to you before. As for the Shaykh's saying "and a clause may not both have a grammatical position and have no grammatical position" to the end of his words, it is all one thing with no additional meaning in it.
[Translator's note: The source reads «لأنه يريد جملة الجواب فقط البتة» ("because he means the answer clause alone, at all"); a negation («لا») has evidently dropped out, since the sentence continues «إنما يريد الجملة القسمية برُمَّتها». The translation follows the evident sense.]
His saying, Exalted is He: {أَجْمَعِينَ} is a tawkīd (emphasis). Know that, most commonly, أجمع and its sisters used for emphasis are brought only after «كل», as in: {فَسَجَدَ الملائكة كُلُّهُمْ أَجْمَعُونَ} [al-Ḥijr: 30]; less commonly they may come without «كل», as in this noble verse, for «أجمعين» is an emphasis of «منكم». Its parallel in what I have mentioned to you is also His saying, Exalted is He: {وَإِنَّ جَهَنَّمَ لَمَوْعِدُهُمْ أَجْمَعِينَ} [al-Ḥijr: 43].

semin-durr:19-19.t:
And in al-Baqara: {رَغَداً}: it is omitted [here] because the speech indicates it.
[Translator's note: The entry is fragmentary in the source; it refers to «رَغَداً», which appears in the parallel verse of al-Baqara (35) but is absent from this verse.]

semin-durr:20-20.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: {فَوَسْوَسَ لَهُمَا}, i.e.: he performed the whispering for their sake. The difference between وسوس له and وسوس إليه is that وسوس له means "for his sake", as stated, and وسوس إليه means "he cast the whispering to him".
الوَسْوَسَة is hidden, repeated speech; similar to it is الوَسْواس, which is the sound of jewellery. الوَسْوَسة is also an evil passing thought. وسوس does not pass to an object; rather it is intransitive. One says: رجل مُوَسْوِس ("an obsessed man") with kasra on the wāw, and it is not said with fatḥa; Ibn al-Aʿrābī said so. Others said: one says مُوَسْوَس له and مُوَسْوَس إليه. Al-Layth said: "al-Waswasa is the talk of the soul, and the hidden sound of a wind shaking reeds and the like, like a whisper." The Exalted said: {وَنَعْلَمُ مَا تُوَسْوِسُ بِهِ نَفْسُهُ} [Qāf: 16]. Ruʾba ibn al-ʿAjjāj said, describing a hunter:
2163 - وَسْوَسَ يدعو مُخلِصاً ربِّ الفَلَق ... لمَّا دَنا الصيد دنا مِنَ الوَهَقْ
(He whispered, sincerely calling on the Lord of the daybreak; when the game drew near, he drew near the lasso.)
i.e.: when he intended the game, he whispered within himself: will he miss or hit? Al-Azharī said: "وسوس and وَزْوَزَ have one meaning."
[Translator's note: The verse number appears in the source as «216 - 3-», evidently a misprint for 2163.]
His saying: {لِيُبْدِيَ}: Concerning this lām there are two views; the more apparent is that it is the lām of cause in its original sense, because that was Satan's aim. Some said: the lām is of outcome and consequence (ṣayrūra, ʿāqiba), because Satan did not know that they would be punished with this particular punishment; so the meaning is that their affair would end up at that. The answer: it is possible that he knew that by one of the means mentioned earlier at His saying {وَلاَ تَجِدُ أَكْثَرَهُمْ شَاكِرِينَ} [al-Aʿrāf: 17].
His saying: {مَا وُورِيَ}: «ما» is a relative meaning "that which", and it is the object of «يُبدي», i.e.: to make manifest that which was concealed. The majority read «وُوْري» with two plain wāws; it is a past verb in the passive; its origin is وارَى, like ضارب; when it was made passive the alif was changed into wāw, as in ضُوْرِبَ. So the first wāw is the fāʾ [first radical] and the second is additional. ʿAbd Allāh [ibn Masʿūd] read: أُوْرِيَ, changing the first into hamza; it is a permissible substitution, not an obligatory one. This is a general rule, namely: when two wāws come together at the beginning of a word, and the second is vowelled or has a vowelled counterpart, the first must be changed into hamza for lightness. Example of the first kind: «أُوَيصل» and «أواصل», the diminutive and broken plural of واصل, whose originals are وُوَيْصِل and وواصل; two wāws came together in both examples, the second of them vowelled, so the first had to be changed into hamza. Example of the second kind: أُوْلى, whose origin is وُوْلَى; the second is quiescent, but it is vowelled in the plural when you say أُوَل, like فُضْلى and فُضَل. If it is not vowelled and is not treated like a vowelled one, the substitution is permissible, as in this noble verse; similar is وُوْطِئ and أُوْطِئ.
Yaḥyā ibn Waththāb read «وُرِيَ» with one wāw bearing ḍamma and a rāʾ with kasra; it is as though it were from the transitive triliteral, and it needs a transmission that وَرَيْتُ كذا means وارَيْتُه.
المُواراة is concealment; from it is his saying, peace be upon him, when the death of Abū Ṭālib reached him: «لعلِّي أذهب مُوارٍ» [Translator's note: so in the source; the wording of this report is uncertain]; and from it is another's saying:
2164 - على صَدىً أسودَ المُواري ... في التُّرْب أمسى وفي الصفيح
([Weeping] over a dark corpse, concealed in the earth, lying under the slabs.)
The verification of this root has been given before.
The majority read «سَوْءاتهما» in the plural, without transfer [of the hamza's vowel] or assimilation.
Mujāhid and al-Ḥasan read «سَوَّتِهما» in the singular, changing the hamza into wāw and assimilating the wāw into it. Al-Ḥasan also, Abū Jaʿfar and Shayba ibn Niṣāḥ read «سَوَّاتِهما» in the plural with the wāw doubled, by the process mentioned. He also read سَواتِهما, likewise in the plural, except that he transferred the hamza's vowel to the wāw without any other process. All of that is clear. As for the one who read the plural, it admits two views. The more apparent: that it is of the type of putting the plural in the place of the dual, from dislike of two duals coming together, the plural being the brother of the dual and so taking its place, as in His saying {صَغَتْ قُلُوبُكُمَا} [al-Taḥrīm: 4]; the verification of this rule has been given before. It may be that the plural here is in its real sense, because each of the two has a front and a back, and السَّوْءات is a euphemism for that, so they are four; hence the plural was brought. The singular reading supports the first, since it is so only when the place is one of the dual, as in: «مَسَح أذنيه ظاهرَهما وباطنهما» ("he wiped his two ears, their outside and their inside").
His saying: {إِلاَّ أَنْ تَكُونَا}: an emptied exception (istithnāʾ mufarragh), and it is a mafʿūl min ajlihi (object of purpose). The Basrans construe it as "except out of dislike that you two become", and the Kufans construe it as "except that you two not become". It has been stated more than once that the Basrans' view is preferable, because implying a noun is better than implying a particle.
The majority read «مَلَكَيْن» with fatḥa on the lām ("two angels"). Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Yaḥyā ibn Abī Kathīr, al-Zuhrī and Ibn Ḥakīm from Ibn Kathīr read «مَلِكين» with kasra ("two kings"). They said: this reading is supported by His saying in another place: {هَلْ أَدُلُّكَ على شَجَرَةِ الخلد وَمُلْكٍ لاَّ يبلى} [Ṭā Hā: 120], and "kingship" suits "king" with kasra. He brought His saying «من الخالدين» and did not say «أو تكونا خالدَيْن» for intensification in that, because description by immortality is more important than being a king or kingship; for your saying «فلان من الصالحين» ("so-and-so is among the righteous") is more emphatic than your saying "righteous"; on this is {وَكَانَتْ مِنَ القانتين} [al-Taḥrīm: 12].

semin-durr:21-21.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: {وقَاسَمَهُمَا}: The mufāʿala (reciprocal form) here may be in its proper sense. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "It is as though he said to them: 'I swear to you that I am among the sincere advisers', and they said to him: 'Do you swear by Allah that you are among our sincere advisers?' So that was made a mutual swearing between them. Or: he swore to them of sincere advice and they swore to him of accepting it. Or: Iblīs's oath was put on the pattern of mufāʿala because he exerted himself in it with the exertion of one engaged in mutual swearing." Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "وقاسمهما, i.e. he swore to them; it is mufāʿala, since the acceptance of the one sworn to and his turning towards the meaning of the oath is like swearing and confirming it, even if at first sight it gives the impression of coming from one party." And it may be that fāʿala has the meaning of afʿala, as in باعَدْته and أبعدته, since the swearing was from Iblīs alone and not from them. On this is the saying of Khālid ibn Zuhayr:
2165 - وقاسَمَها بالله جَهْداً لأنتمُ ... ألذَّ مِنَ السَّلوى إذا ما نشورها
(And he swore to her by Allah with all his effort: you are sweeter than honey when we gather it.)
His saying: {لَكُمَا لَمِنَ النَّاصِحِين}: As for «لكما», it may be attached (mutaʿalliq) to what follows it, on the basis that al is the definite article and not a relative; this is the position of Abū ʿUthmān [al-Māzinī]. Or on the basis that it is the relative, but leeway is given with the adverb and its equivalent [the prepositional phrase] that is not given with others, as a widening of their use because they occur so often in speech; this is the opinion of some Basrans, and he recited:
2166 - رَبَّيْتُهُ حتى إذا تَمَعْدَدا ... كان جزائي بالعصا أن أُجْلدا
(I raised him until, when he grew sturdy, my reward was to be flogged with the stick.)
So «بالعصا» is attached to أُجْلَد, which is the ṣila of أَنْ. Or that this is permissible absolutely, even with an explicit direct object; this is the opinion of the Kufans, and they recited:
2167 -. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... وشفاءُ غَيِّك خابِراً أن تسألي
(…and the cure of your ignorance is that you ask one who knows.)
i.e.: أن تسألي خابراً. Or it is attached to something omitted by way of clarification, i.e.: I mean, for you two — as in their saying سقياً لك ورَعياً ("may you be watered and protected"). Or it is attached to something omitted indicated by the ṣila of al, i.e.: I am an adviser to you. Like this noble verse are: {إِنِّي لِعَمَلِكُمْ مِّنَ القالين} [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 168] and {وَكَانُواْ فِيهِ مِنَ الزاهدين} [Yūsuf: 20]. Ibn Mālik made this regular in the question of the relative al when it is in the genitive with مِنْ.
نَصَح takes one object, sometimes by itself and sometimes through a preposition; similar to it is شكر, which has been dealt with, and كال and وزن. Is the original the transitivity through a preposition, or the transitivity by itself, or is each of them original? The preferred view is the third. Some claimed that the object in these verbs is omitted, and that what is in the genitive with the lām is the second [object]; so if you say نصحتُ لزيدٍ, the implied form is: I gave Zayd sincere counsel (نصحت لزيد الرأيَ); likewise شَكَر له صنيعه, كِلْتُ له طعامه and وَزَنْتُ له متاعه. This is a fourth position. Al-Farrāʾ said: "The Arabs hardly say نصحتك; they only say نصحتُ لك and أنصح لك"; yet نصحتك may be allowed. Al-Nābigha said:
2168 - نصحتُ بني عوفٍ فلم يتقبَّلوا ... رسولي ولم تنجحْ لديهم وسائلي
(I advised the Banū ʿAwf, but they did not receive my messenger, and my approaches to them did not succeed.)
This strengthens the view that the lām is original.
[Translator's note: The quotation from al-Farrāʾ seems to support the lām being original, whereas the verse of al-Nābigha is an instance without lām; the source's wording is translated as it stands.]
النُّصْح is expending effort in seeking good specifically; its opposite is deceit. As for «نصحت لزيد ثوبه», it takes two objects, one by itself and the second through a preposition, by agreement. It is as though النصح, which is expending effort in good, is taken from one of two meanings: either from نَصَح meaning "made pure", from which is ناصح العسل, i.e. pure honey, so that "he advised him sincerely" means he made his affection pure for him; or from نَصَحْتُ الجِلْد والثوب, when you sew the leather and the garment firmly, from which is الناصح for the tailor and النِّصاح for the thread; so "he advised him" means he made firm his counsel for him. One says: نَصَحه نُصوحاً ونَصاحة. The Exalted said: {توبوا إِلَى الله تَوْبَةً نَّصُوحاً} [al-Taḥrīm: 8], with ḍamma on the nūn in the reading of Abū Bakr [Shuʿba]. The poet said, regarding «نَصاحة»:
2169 - أَحْبَبْتُ حُبَّاً خالَطَتْه نَصاحةٌ ... . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
(I loved with a love mingled with sincerity…)
That is like ذُهوب and ذَهاب.

semin-durr:22-22.t:
